title: Ozymandias read by Werner Herzog — archive and decay as film theme
summary: Werner Herzog reads Shelley's 'Ozymandias' as the hook for Sandbox Films' documentary 'The Arc of Oblivion', about why humans build records that will inevitably fade. Worth it as a study in voice, pacing and pairing classic text with documentary imagery.
takeaways: Pairing a canonical poem with a distinctive narrator gives a film trailer instant gravity
The film's theme (archives in nature and culture) is a reusable framing for creative projects

title: Elizabeth Greenshields Foundation — no-deadline CAD 17k grant for early painters
summary: The Elizabeth Greenshields Foundation gives CAD 17,000 first grants (20,000 on renewal) to early-career representational artists worldwide, with no fee, no CV and rolling applications by post. The Awesome Foundation's $1,000 monthly micro-grants (US, UK, Australia, Canada chapters) are the fallback for abstract or non-painting work.
takeaways: Greenshields: representational work only (painting, drawing, sculpture, printmaking), application must be printed, signed and mailed
No deadline and open worldwide, roughly 93 artists funded last year
Awesome Foundation chapters give $1,000/month with near-zero eligibility bar

title: Cozy multiplayer browser game — open-world mail delivery on a tiny planet
summary: An unnamed free browser game where you customize a character and deliver messages across a small Japanese-street-styled planet, with live multiplayer. Fun as a reference for what WebGL in the browser can do, but the post never names the site.
takeaways: Browser-native 3D multiplayer worlds are viable without installs
Site name not given in the post, you would have to search for it

title: Turing patterns — why reaction-diffusion gives us five fingers
summary: Philip Ball (Royal Institution talk) explains that digit count is set during embryonic development by Alan Turing's 1952 reaction-diffusion mechanism: interacting chemical signals self-organize into regular stripes that become fingers. The Whisper transcript is garbled, so the caption and the known Turing model carry the content.
takeaways: Reaction-diffusion (Turing, 1952) explains periodic patterns like digits, stripes and spots
The same equations are a staple of generative art and shader experiments

title: The NeverEnding Story — the Nothing as a metaphor for lost hope
summary: A clip from The NeverEnding Story (1984) where the Nothing is explained as the despair left when people abandon their dreams, because people without hope are easy to control. Nostalgia and mood reference, no technique.
takeaways: A short, quotable framing of hope versus control from a classic film

title: DeepPIV laser-sheet scanning — 3D models of deep-sea siphonophores in situ
summary: Schmidt Ocean Institute's ROV on the Falkor (too) uses MBARI's DeepPIV system: a laser flattened into a thin sheet is swept through semi-transparent animals to capture planes that stack into full 3D reconstructions, without killing the specimen. The subject is a siphonophore, a colony of specialized zooids acting as one animal.
takeaways: Sweeping a planar laser through a transparent subject yields slice stacks you can reconstruct in 3D
Non-destructive in-situ scanning beats collecting fragile specimens
Visual reference for volumetric, glowing organic forms

title: Crystal Pite's The Seasons' Canon — contemporary ballet of mass ensemble motion
summary: Crystal Pite's 'The Seasons' Canon' (Paris Opera Ballet, 2016, set to Max Richter's Vivaldi recomposition), back at Palais Garnier. Worth studying for how a large ensemble moves as one organism.
takeaways: Ensemble motion as a single organism is a strong reference for crowd and particle animation
Pite is a go-to choreographer for kinetic composition

title: Jim Simons and the Riemann Hypothesis — the benchmark for AI math claims
summary: Anecdote about Renaissance Technologies founder Jim Simons lighting up when asked if he'd trade his fortune to solve the Riemann Hypothesis, used to argue that RH has become the gold-standard test people demand of AI math systems. Light commentary, no technical depth.
takeaways: Medallion Fund lore: worst year reportedly around +20%
Public sentiment treats RH as the bar for AI mathematical capability

title: HFT short-term reversal — buy weekly losers, sell winners across 4,500 stocks
summary: A 60 Minutes clip with Manoj Narang describing a cross-sectional mean-reversion test: buy $5 of stocks down 5% last week, sell $10 of stocks up 10%, across the whole ~4,500-stock universe at once. Near 50% win rate per trade but no losing month thanks to breadth and speed, with Joe Saluzzi arguing it rigs the game.
takeaways: Edge comes from breadth: tiny edges over thousands of names, not stock picking
Position size proportional to the move is a simple reversal weighting
Win rate near 50% can still compound if exposure is diversified and cheap to execute

title: Efficiency-ratio forecaster — skip choppy days to lift a strategy's metrics
summary: Instead of predicting direction, a logistic regression on 15 price features forecasts the next day's Kaufman efficiency ratio (trendiness versus chop). Trades on predicted low-efficiency days made about a third of the money, so gating them out improved nearly every metric and held on two years of out-of-sample data.
takeaways: Predict the regime (trend vs chop), not the direction, and use it as a trade filter
Split existing trades by the predicted regime to validate the signal before gating
Confirm on unseen data; here it held for two years out of sample

title: Overnight vs intraday returns — Knuteson's 'Strikingly Suspicious' anomaly
summary: Bruce Knuteson (ex-MIT physicist, D. E. Shaw) splits each day into close-to-open and open-to-close: Micron since 1990 is +138M% overnight and -99.9% intraday, and the same sawtooth shows in 21 indices (China reversed). His paper 'Strikingly Suspicious Overnight and Intraday Returns' rejects earnings and news as explanations and alleges large firms push prices at the open; it's a claim, not a proof.
takeaways: Decompose returns into overnight and intraday legs; the two compound to buy-and-hold
Pattern holds across 21 global indices, so it's not a single-stock artifact
Trading costs and gaps at the open matter before treating this as a strategy
Paper: Knuteson, 'Strikingly Suspicious Overnight and Intraday Returns' (arXiv, 2020)

title: PBEMA TradingView indicator — trend-filter buy/sell line on the S&P 500
summary: Promo for a free TradingView indicator (PBEMA): buy when price is above a moving-average line, sell below, claimed to outperform buy-and-hold on the S&P 500 since 1930 by sidestepping 2000 and 2008. The Munger attribution and the personal P&L claims are unverified, and the link is gated behind a comment.
takeaways: A long-term moving-average filter mainly helps by avoiding big drawdowns, at the cost of whipsaws
Treat the Munger quote and returns as marketing until you backtest it

title: 2010 Flash Crash — how Navinder Sarao spoofed E-mini S&P futures
summary: Story of the May 6, 2010 Flash Crash (about 9% in minutes, $1T wiped then recovered), traced to Navinder Sarao spoofing E-mini S&P 500 futures from his bedroom with large sell orders he cancelled, tricking algos into selling. Good primer on spoofing and cascading algorithmic selling.
takeaways: Spoofed order-book pressure can trigger cascades in algos that read depth
Exchange and bank safeguards were the real failure point

title: Claude multi-agent trading team — research, market, backtest and risk agents
summary: Pitch for an unnamed free repo that spins Claude into a four-agent trading team: a research agent cleans market data, a market agent writes strategy logic, a test agent backtests for win rate and max drawdown, and a risk agent audits for self-deception. The repo is never named; the link is gated behind a comment.
takeaways: The role split (data, logic, backtest, risk audit) is a sensible template for any agent trading pipeline
A dedicated adversarial risk agent guards against overfitting

title: Charlie Munger's inversion — solve problems by asking how to cause failure
summary: Munger explains inversion with his WWII meteorologist job: ask how you'd kill pilots (icing, running out of fuel), then avoid those. Same move for any problem: list what would hurt it most and steer clear.
takeaways: Reframe 'how do I succeed' as 'what would guarantee failure' and avoid those paths
Works for system design and risk reviews as well as investing
Pairs naturally with pre-mortems

title: Katsuyama vs BATS on CNBC — the 'markets are rigged' HFT showdown
summary: The March 31, 2014 CNBC clash where IEX's Brad Katsuyama (Flash Boys) accused exchanges of selling HFT advantages via direct feeds, co-location and complex order types, and BATS's Bill O'Brien was pressed on whether his matching engine priced off the slower SIP. BATS later corrected the record, and IEX's speed bump came out of this debate.
takeaways: Direct feeds vs the SIP latency gap is the core of latency arbitrage
IEX's speed bump is a design response worth understanding
Order types and data feeds shape who wins on an exchange

title: Chip stock selloff rumor — a fund blowup and the Intel overhang
summary: Market chatter tying a recent chip-stock selloff to a fund blowup by a trader famous for an Intel bet, with Ken Griffin reportedly absorbing the book off-market. Unsourced rumor plus generic macro commentary (yen, CDS, Kevin Warsh).
takeaways: Unsourced; treat as sentiment color, not information

title: Kronos — open-source foundation model trained on 12B candlesticks
summary: Survey of zero-shot time-series foundation models (Google TimesFM 2.5, Amazon Chronos, Salesforce Moirai, IBM Tiny Time Mixers) that mostly fail at stock prediction, then Kronos: an open-source model pre-trained on about 12 billion K-lines from crypto and other markets that beats prior models on financial forecasting. Code on GitHub and Hugging Face from shiyu-coder.
takeaways: Generic time-series foundation models barely beat simple autoregressive baselines on stocks
Kronos is domain-pretrained on candlesticks and is open source
Pair any forecast with portfolio optimization, risk neutralization and cost control

title: Warsh, the Clarity Act and tokenized stocks — crypto-rails news roundup
summary: Hype-framed roundup: Kevin Warsh confirmed as Fed chair, the Clarity Act clearing Senate Banking 15-9, NYSE using Securitize for tokenized stocks, Nasdaq tokenizing the Russell 1000 and BlackRock filing tokenized funds. Ends in a comment-for-training funnel, so verify each claim yourself.
takeaways: Headline items worth checking: Clarity Act status, NYSE/Securitize, Nasdaq tokenization approval
Funnel post; the framing is promotional

title: Bollinger Bands + RSI kid trader — satire of trading-course culture
summary: Comedy skit mocking influencer trading courses: a 'first-grader' fumbles a Bollinger Bands plus RSI setup and still hits take-profit. Entertainment, not instruction.
takeaways: A reminder that one winning trade proves nothing about a setup

title: Quant/ML project reel — repo links gated, no content
summary: Silent reel with a 'comment Repo' caption and no transcript, OCR or named projects.
drop_reason: no subject: silent video, caption is pure engagement bait with no named project

title: Fundrise VCX at 25x NAV — cheaper proxies for private AI and space names
summary: Fundrise's newly listed VCX closed-end fund trades around 25x its net asset value (about a 2,000% premium). Cheaper exposures named instead: Kraken Robotics as an Anduril supplier, Amazon for its Anthropic stake, and a Canadian private-asset fund near 1x NAV for OpenAI and SpaceX exposure.
takeaways: Always compare a listed fund's price to its NAV before buying hype
Public proxies (suppliers, stakeholders) can give private-company exposure at fair value

title: Regular Show's 'Synth Wars' — synthesizer battle as cosmic boss fight
summary: The climax of Regular Show's 'Gary's Synthesizer', where two half-brothers settle a throne dispute with a synth battle (discord vs harmony) that escalates into a cosmic boss fight. Fun reference for music-driven animated set pieces.
takeaways: Dissonance vs harmony as a visual-musical conflict is a reusable storytelling device
